cues.text: A Life Thrown Away in Alexandria
Long before she was known as a saint, tradition holds that Mary left her family in Egypt at the age of twelve.
She made her way to Alexandria, where for the next seventeen years she gave herself over completely to a life of dissolute pleasure.
The account handed down of her life records that she pursued this life not chiefly out of need.
Instead, she followed what she herself later called the fire of her own passions, refusing even payment for her favors so that nothing might interrupt them.
It is a stark opening to a story the Church has never softened, precisely because everything that follows depends on the completeness of what came before.
A Door That Would Not Open
Drawn one day, tradition relates, more by curiosity and the prospect of company than by any religious motive, Mary joined a crowd of pilgrims.
They sailed from Alexandria to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, and she continued her former way of life throughout the voyage.

At the church in Jerusalem, however, she found herself unable to cross the threshold; an unseen force, the account says, held her back each time she tried to enter with the crowd, while everyone around her passed through freely.
Struck to the heart, she turned to a statue of the Blessed Virgin standing nearby.
In that moment of shame and confusion, she made a vow: if allowed to enter and venerate the True Cross, she would leave the world behind forever and go wherever Our Lady might lead her.
Seventeen Years Alone Among Wild Beasts
She was permitted to enter.
Keeping her vow, Mary crossed the Jordan River into the wilderness beyond it and did not return.
She lived entirely alone for what tradition records as roughly forty-seven years, sustained by little more than the desert itself provided and by a hunger for penance that never relented.
She later told the monk who found her that the hardest years were the first.
Memories of her former life rose up against her like wild beasts, to be fought and mastered one by one.
Her soul was finally purified of them by unceasing prayer and solitude.
An Old Monk's Encounter in the Wilderness
Near the end of her life, an elderly monk named Zosimas lived at a Palestinian monastery near the Jordan.
According to his community’s custom, he had gone alone into the desert during Lent and encountered a figure weathered by sun and years of exposure.
He could scarcely tell whether it was a man or a woman.
Despite having lived without human contact for decades, she recognized him as a priest and asked him for his mantle to cover herself.
At his pleading, she then recounted to him the whole of her life exactly as it had been, sparing herself nothing.

Before they parted, she asked one thing of him: that he return the following year, on Holy Thursday, and bring her Holy Communion, which she had not received since the day she first crossed the Jordan.
Communion on the Banks of the Jordan
Zosimas returned the following Lent as she had asked, carrying the Blessed Sacrament to the riverbank.
Tradition holds that Mary appeared on the far shore, made the sign of the cross over the water, and walked across its surface to meet him.
After nearly five decades apart from Holy Communion, she received it and lifted her hands.
She cried out in the words of the aged Simeon: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace, because my eyes have seen thy salvation."
She asked Zosimas to return once more the following year to the place where they had first met.
When he did, he found her body, with a message traced in the sand asking for burial and revealing that she had died on the very night of her Communion the year before.
Legacy
The account of St. Mary of Egypt was set down some generations later.
Tradition attributes it to St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem.
It has been read in Lenten liturgies East and West ever since—not to hold up an extraordinary sinner as an oddity, but to show every ordinary sinner what conversion can still accomplish.
We recognize in her both extremes of the human heart: seventeen years spent in the deepest exile from God.
Forty-seven more were spent in a penance so complete that, at the very end, her only remaining hunger was for the Bread that once again would make her whole.
Few saints witness so starkly to the truth that no distance from God lies beyond the reach of His mercy, or beyond the Eucharist's power to complete what that mercy begins.
